title: Helminths That Harm the Host: Strongyloides Hyperinfection, Hookworm Blood Loss, Fish Tapeworm B12 and Fluke Drugs
summary: Learn why Strongyloides hyperinfection follows immunosuppression and how screening and ivermectin prevent it, how hookworms cause iron-deficiency anaemia, how the broad fish tapeworm lowers vitamin B12, and why praziquantel treats flukes except Fasciola.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 65 Hits 6, 9, 13 and 14. Strongyloides from Czeresnia 2022, Luvira 2022 and the Cochrane review Henriquez-Camacho 2016; hookworm from Brooker 2004 and Hotez 2005 (both read via a page-fetch tool); broad fish tapeworm from Scholz 2009 (read via a page-fetch tool), Leštinová 2016 and Radačovská 2019; flukes from Caravedo 2020, Gandhi 2019, Chai 2022 and Bergquist 2017. Hit 9 gives A. duodenale blood loss as 0.15–0.25 mL/day; Brooker 2004 gives 0.15 mL (range 0.14–0.30) and N. americanus 0.03 mL (range 0.01–0.04) (register flag rv-hookworm-blood-loss-range). Hit 13 states that Diphyllobothrium causes B12 deficiency (megaloblastic anaemia); Scholz 2009 reports low B12 in about 40% and clinical anaemia in 2% or fewer (register flag rv-dlatum-b12-minority); the type species is now placed in the resurrected genus Dibothriocephalus (register flag rv-dlatum-genus-renamed). Not taught: hookworm treatment, Ascaris formalin safety (Hit 15), moxidectin, drug doses.

objectives: Explain how immunosuppression, especially corticosteroids, triggers Strongyloides hyperinfection, and state the screening and ivermectin response.
Describe how hookworms cause iron-deficiency anaemia and compare blood loss per worm for Ancylostoma duodenale and Necator americanus.
Describe how the broad fish tapeworm lowers vitamin B12 and how often this causes clinical anaemia.
Choose praziquantel for schistosomes and most flukes, and triclabendazole for Fasciola.

scenes.title: Three worms, three kinds of harm
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: three patients. (1) A man who grew up in a Strongyloides-endemic area takes high-dose prednisone for a lung disease flare; he now has fever, abdominal pain and Escherichia coli in his blood, and larvae are seen in his sputum. (2) A child in a rural endemic area has microcytic anaemia; stool shows hookworm eggs. (3) An adult who often eats raw freshwater fish has low vitamin B12; stool shows operculate eggs. A fourth note: a traveller with liver-fluke eggs needs treatment. Question token: “What did the worm do, and which drug?”

cues.text: Three patients. A man from a Strongyloides area takes high-dose steroids, and now has gut bacteria in his blood and larvae in his sputum.
A child with microcytic anaemia has hookworm eggs in stool. An adult who eats raw fish has low vitamin B12 and capped eggs in stool.
What did each worm do to its host, and which drug treats it?

props.label: What did the worm do, and which drug?

scenes.title: How two worms drain the host
scenes.altText: Schematic cards. Hookworm (Brooker 2004; Hotez 2005): adults attach to the intestinal mucosa, rupture capillaries and secrete anticoagulant and anti-platelet molecules, so blood oozes continuously; the worm ingests blood and digests haemoglobin. Blood loss rises with worm burden; in heavy infection or low iron stores the result is iron-deficiency, microcytic hypochromic anaemia. Estimated loss per worm per day: Ancylostoma duodenale about 0.15 mL (range 0.14–0.30), Necator americanus about 0.03 mL (range 0.01–0.04), so A. duodenale causes roughly five times more per worm. Broad fish tapeworm (Diphyllobothrium latum, now placed in the genus Dibothriocephalus): acquired by eating raw or undercooked fish; the worm absorbs about 80% of dietary vitamin B12 and splits the B12–intrinsic factor complex; about 40% of infected people have low B12 but 2% or fewer develop clinical (megaloblastic) anaemia. Eggs: thick-shelled, unembryonated, operculum at the narrower end and a knob at the opposite end.

cues.text: Hookworms bite into the gut lining, break small vessels and release anticoagulants, so blood keeps oozing. The worms swallow blood and digest the haemoglobin.

The more worms, the more blood lost. With heavy infection or poor iron stores, the result is iron-deficiency anaemia: small, pale red cells. Per worm, Ancylostoma duodenale loses about zero point one five millilitres a day, Necator about zero point zero three: roughly five times less.
The broad fish tapeworm comes from raw or undercooked fish. It soaks up most of the vitamin B12 in the diet and splits B12 from intrinsic factor.
About forty percent of infected people have low B12, but two percent or fewer develop megaloblastic anaemia. Its eggs are unembryonated, with a lid at one end and a small knob at the other.

scenes.title: When Strongyloides turns deadly
scenes.altText: Hyperinfection card (Czeresnia 2022; Luvira 2022): Strongyloides stercoralis completes autoinfection inside the host, so chronic infection can persist for life. When the host becomes immunosuppressed, autoinfection accelerates and the parasite burden rises sharply (hyperinfection); larvae carry enteric bacteria, causing recurrent, sometimes polymicrobial, Gram-negative bloodstream infection and meningitis; larvae appear in sputum or bronchoalveolar lavage. Triggers: corticosteroids are the most common (courses as short as 6 days and doses as low as 20 mg prednisone per day reported); also HTLV-1 infection, haematological malignancy, transplantation, hypogammaglobulinaemia and other immunosuppressants. Eosinophilia is usually absent because steroids are the usual trigger. Untreated hyperinfection mortality 85–100%. Screening card: people with exposure in endemic areas who will become immunosuppressed should be screened (serology, stool parasitology) and treated before immunosuppression.

cues.text: Strongyloides can re-infect its host from inside the gut, so an infection picked up decades ago can persist silently for life.

If the host becomes immunosuppressed, that autoinfection speeds up and the worm burden explodes. Larvae carry gut bacteria into the blood, causing Gram-negative sepsis and even meningitis, and larvae appear in sputum.

Corticosteroids are the most common trigger, even short courses or modest doses. HTLV-1, blood cancers and transplantation also raise the risk. Eosinophilia is often absent, and untreated hyperinfection is usually fatal.
So people with exposure in endemic areas should be screened, with serology and stool tests, and treated before immunosuppression starts.

scenes.title: The right drug for each worm
scenes.altText: Drug cards. Strongyloides: ivermectin is the drug of choice; a Cochrane review found more people cured with ivermectin than with albendazole, with similar tolerability (Henriquez-Camacho 2016); for hyperinfection, experts suggest ivermectin daily for at least two weeks and reducing immunosuppression where possible (Czeresnia 2022). Flukes: praziquantel is the drug of choice for schistosomiasis (Bergquist 2017) and is used for Clonorchis, Opisthorchis, paragonimiasis and intestinal flukes (Chai 2022); it also treats the broad fish tapeworm (Scholz 2009). Exception card: Fasciola — praziquantel is not effective; triclabendazole is the drug of choice, recommended by WHO (Caravedo 2020; Gandhi 2019; Chai 2022). Hook answers: (1) Strongyloides hyperinfection → ivermectin, reduce steroids; (2) hookworm iron-deficiency anaemia; (3) fish tapeworm B12 deficiency → praziquantel; liver fluke → identify Fasciola before choosing praziquantel.

cues.text: Strongyloides: ivermectin is the drug of choice. A Cochrane review found it cures more people than albendazole. In hyperinfection, experts give it daily for at least two weeks and cut back immunosuppression if possible.
Flukes: praziquantel is the drug of choice for schistosomiasis and treats the Chinese and cat liver flukes, lung flukes and intestinal flukes. It also clears the broad fish tapeworm.
The exception is Fasciola, the sheep liver fluke. Praziquantel does not work against it; triclabendazole is the drug of choice.

Back to the hook: ivermectin and less steroid for the first patient; iron-deficiency anaemia from hookworm for the child; praziquantel for the fish tapeworm. And for a liver fluke, name the species before choosing the drug.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “No eosinophilia, so no Strongyloides hyperinfection” (✓ eosinophilia is often absent because steroids are the usual trigger); “Praziquantel treats every fluke” (✓ not Fasciola, which needs triclabendazole); “Fish tapeworm always causes megaloblastic anaemia” (✓ about 40% have low B12, 2% or fewer develop clinical anaemia).

cues.text: Trap one: no eosinophilia, so it cannot be Strongyloides hyperinfection. No: steroids, the usual trigger, often suppress eosinophils.
Trap two: praziquantel treats every fluke. No: Fasciola needs triclabendazole.
Trap three: the fish tapeworm always causes megaloblastic anaemia. No: low B12 is common, but clinical anaemia is rare.

scenes.title: Vampire, thief, squatter, rebel
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “The hookworm is a VAMPIRE (sips blood → iron deficiency; Ancylostoma takes the bigger sip). The fish tapeworm is a B12 THIEF. Strongyloides is a SQUATTER that breeds indoors and takes over when the guards (immunity) leave: screen before steroids, evict with ivermectin. Praziquantel is the fluke key, but Fasciola is the REBEL lock: use triclabendazole.” Tokens. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: the hookworm is a vampire, and Ancylostoma takes the bigger sip. The fish tapeworm is a B12 thief. Strongyloides is a squatter that breeds indoors and takes over when the guards leave: screen before steroids, evict with ivermectin. Praziquantel is the fluke key, but Fasciola is the rebel lock.

Where it breaks: each worm sips only a fraction of a millilitre, so anaemia depends on worm numbers and iron stores; the thief rarely causes clinical anaemia; and hyperinfection can occasionally occur without obvious immunosuppression.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Strongyloides: screen before immunosuppression · ivermectin · eosinophilia may be absent”, “Hookworm → iron-deficiency anaemia · fish tapeworm → low B12 · praziquantel for flukes except Fasciola (triclabendazole)”.

cues.text: Screen people with endemic exposure for Strongyloides before immunosuppression and treat with ivermectin, link hookworm to iron-deficiency anaemia and the fish tapeworm to low vitamin B12, and use praziquantel for flukes except Fasciola, which needs triclabendazole.

props.label: Hookworm → iron deficiency · fish tapeworm → B12 · Fasciola → triclabendazole

explanation.what: Plain language: some worms harm people in a specific way. Hookworms drink blood from the gut wall, so people lose iron. The fish tapeworm steals vitamin B12. Strongyloides can live in a person for decades and suddenly multiply out of control when the immune system is suppressed. The usual fluke drug, praziquantel, does not work on one liver fluke, Fasciola. Scientific terms: Strongyloides stercoralis, autoinfection, hyperinfection syndrome, disseminated strongyloidiasis, ivermectin, Ancylostoma duodenale, Necator americanus, iron-deficiency (microcytic hypochromic) anaemia, Diphyllobothrium (Dibothriocephalus) latum, vitamin B12–intrinsic factor complex, megaloblastic anaemia, praziquantel, Fasciola hepatica, triclabendazole.
explanation.why: Strongyloides autoinfection lets a small chronic infection expand when immunity falls; corticosteroids are the most common trigger. Hookworm anticoagulants keep the attachment site bleeding, and blood loss scales with worm burden. The fish tapeworm absorbs dietary B12 and dissociates it from intrinsic factor. Fasciola does not respond to praziquantel.
explanation.measure: Hyperinfection: larvae in sputum, bronchoalveolar lavage or other fluids; recurrent enteric Gram-negative bacteraemia; eosinophilia often absent. Screening: serology and stool parasitology. Hookworm: about 0.15 mL/worm/day (A. duodenale) vs 0.03 mL (N. americanus). Fish tapeworm: low B12 in about 40%, clinical anaemia in 2% or fewer; operculate unembryonated eggs with a knob at the opposite end.
explanation.differs: Chronic strongyloidiasis vs hyperinfection; A. duodenale vs N. americanus blood loss; iron-deficiency (hookworm) vs B12-deficiency (fish tapeworm) anaemia; praziquantel-responsive flukes vs Fasciola.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: screening before steroids for patients from endemic areas, ivermectin as drug of choice, Gram-negative sepsis and larvae in sputum in hyperinfection, which hookworm bleeds more, the anaemia type for each worm, and triclabendazole for fascioliasis.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old who grew up in a Strongyloides-endemic region is about to start high-dose corticosteroids. What is the best step?

options.text: Screen for Strongyloides (serology and stool) and treat with ivermectin if positive before immunosuppression
options.rationale: Correct. Chronic infection can persist for decades and corticosteroids are the most common trigger of hyperinfection.

options.text: No screening is needed unless eosinophilia is present
options.rationale: Incorrect. Chronic infection can be silent, and eosinophilia is often absent, especially on steroids.
Incorrect. Praziquantel is a fluke and tapeworm drug; ivermectin is the drug of choice for Strongyloides.

options.text: A single stool ova-and-parasite exam that is negative excludes infection
options.rationale: Incorrect. Chronic infection has few larvae; screening combines serology and parasitological tests.

questions.stem: Which statement about hookworm-related anaemia is correct?

options.text: It is iron-deficiency anaemia from intestinal blood loss, and Ancylostoma duodenale loses more blood per worm than Necator americanus
options.rationale: Correct. Estimates are about 0.15 vs 0.03 mL per worm per day; blood loss rises with worm burden.

options.text: It is megaloblastic anaemia caused by vitamin B12 uptake by the worm
options.rationale: Incorrect. That mechanism belongs to the broad fish tapeworm.

options.text: Necator americanus loses more blood per worm than Ancylostoma duodenale
options.rationale: Incorrect. N. americanus is smaller and causes less blood loss per worm.

options.text: A single worm usually causes severe anaemia
options.rationale: Incorrect. Each worm takes a fraction of a millilitre; anaemia depends on intensity and iron stores.

questions.stem: A patient has Fasciola hepatica infection. Which drug is the treatment of choice?

options.rationale: Correct. Triclabendazole is the drug of choice and the WHO-recommended treatment for fascioliasis.
Incorrect. Praziquantel treats most other flukes but is not effective against Fasciola.
Incorrect. Ivermectin is the drug of choice for Strongyloides, not flukes.
Incorrect. B12 replacement relates to the fish tapeworm and does not treat any helminth.

claims.note: Not taught as stated; the lesson uses Brooker 2004 estimates and Scholz 2009 frequencies (register flags rv-hookworm-blood-loss-range, rv-dlatum-b12-minority).

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 65 Hit 9 gives A. duodenale blood loss as 0.15–0.25 mL/day per worm and a 5–8× ratio; Brooker 2004 gives 0.15 mL (range 0.14–0.30) for A. duodenale and 0.03 mL (range 0.01–0.04) for N. americanus, so the ratio depends on which estimates are used (register flag rv-hookworm-blood-loss-range).

Ch. 65 Hit 13 presents B12 deficiency with megaloblastic anaemia as the consequence of Diphyllobothrium infection; Scholz 2009 reports low B12 in about 40% of infected people and clinical anaemia in 2% or fewer (register flag rv-dlatum-b12-minority).

Diphyllobothrium latum is now placed in the resurrected genus Dibothriocephalus (Dibothriocephalus latus; Radačovská 2019); the reviewer uses only the older name (register flag rv-dlatum-genus-renamed).
